text: The Asahi Shimbun, founded in 1879 in Osaka as a small-print, four-page illustrated paper selling for one sen and initially circulating around 3,000 copies, is one of the oldest and largest national daily newspapers in Japan and Asia. Its founding officers were Kimura Noboru (company president), Murayama Ryōhei (owner), and Tsuda Tei (managing editor), with the first editorial printed on 13 September 1879. In 1881, it adopted an all-news format and enlisted Ueno Riichi as co-owner; from 1882, it received financial support from the government and Mitsui, and under Ueno and Murayama’s leadership, it gained national prominence. On 10 July 1888, the Tokyo Asahi Shimbun was launched at Motosukiyachō, Kyōbashi, numbered as No. 1,076, continuing three earlier papers. In 1881, Ueno Riichi became a co-owner. On 1 April 1907, Natsume Sōseki joined the Tokyo Asahi Shimbun after resigning from Tokyo Imperial University, following the publication of his novels *Wagahai wa Neko de Aru* and *Botchan*. On 1 October 1908, the Osaka and Tokyo editions were merged into Asahi Shimbun Gōshi Kaisha with a capitalization of approximately 600,000 yen. In 1918, the newspaper faced government suppression of an article criticizing Terauchi Masatake’s cabinet during the Rice Riots, leading to a softening of its liberal stance and staff resignations. During the February 26 Incident of 1936 and throughout its history, the Asahi was vandalized and attacked by ultranationalists due to its liberal position. From the 1930s, it supported Prime Minister Fumimaro Konoe’s wartime government (Konoe Shin Taisei) and criticized capitalism under Editor-in-Chief Taketora Ogata. Influential editorial writers such as Shintarō Ryū, Hiroo Sassa, and Hotsumi Ozaki (a spy informant for Richard Sorge) were members of the Shōwa Kenkyūkai, a political think tank for Konoe. Ogata was a leading member of the Genyōsha, an ultranationalist group including Kōki Hirota, who was later executed as a Class A war criminal and a close friend of Ogata. Ryū, formerly a Marxist economist, advocated centrally planned economies in *Nihon Keizai no Saihensei* (1939), while Sassa, son of ultranationalist politician Sassa Tomofusa, allied with far-right generals and terrorists who assassinated Junnosuke Inoue, Dan Takuma, and Inukai Tsuyoshi, and attempted to assassinate Prime Minister Hideki Tōjō in 1944. On 9 April 1937, the Kamikaze, a Mitsubishi aircraft sponsored by Asahi and flown by Masaaki Iinuma, arrived in London, becoming the first Japanese-built aircraft to fly to Europe. On 1 September 1940, the Osaka and Tokyo editions unified under the name Asahi Shimbun. On 1 January 1943, the government halted publication after Seigō Nakano, a Genyōsha member and Ogata’s friend, published a critical essay. On 27 December 1943, Nagataka Murayama, son-in-law of Murayama Ryōhei and Asahi president, removed Ogata from Editor-in-Chief and demoted him to Vice President. On 22 July 1944, Ogata became Minister without Portfolio and President of Cabinet Intelligence Agency in Kuniaki Koiso’s cabinet. On 7 April 1945, Hiroshi Shimomura, former Vice President, held the same position in Kantarō Suzuki’s cabinet. On 17 August 1945, Ogata became Minister without Portfolio, Chief Cabinet Secretary, and President of Cabinet Intelligence Agency in Prince Higashikuni’s cabinet. On 5 November 1945, the Asahi’s president and senior executives resigned en masse to take responsibility for compromising the paper’s principles during the war. On 21 November 1946, the newspaper adopted the modern kana usage system (shin kanazukai). On 30 November 1949, it began publishing the serialized cartoon strip *Sazae-san* by Machiko Hasegawa, a landmark in Japan’s postwar era. Between 1954 and 1971, it published a glossy, large-format annual in English titled *This is Japan*. In April–May 1989, the paper reported that a coral reef near Okinawa was defaced by a man with a dissolute Japanese mind, later revealed to be a fabricated report by the reporter himself, known as the Asahi Shimbun coral article hoax incident; the president resigned. On 26 June 2007, Yoichi Funabashi became the third editor-in-chief. Shōichi Ueno, co-owner since 1997, died on 29 February 2016. Under Shin-ichi Hakojima, the Asahi partnered with the International Herald Tribune to launch the *International Herald Tribune/Asahi Shimbun*, which ran from April 2001 to February 2011, replacing the *Asahi Evening News*; the partnership ended in 2010 due to unprofitability, and the Asahi now operates the Asia & Japan Watch online portal for English readers. The Tribune (now The International New York Times) collaborates with Asahi on Aera English, a glossy magazine for English learners. The Asahi is considered left-leaning, described as “the intellectual flagship of Japan’s political left,” with a tradition of reporting on political scandals more than conservative papers, and is regarded as a newspaper of record in Japan. It criticizes right-wing nationalism and shows progressive views on cultural and diplomatic issues, though it has a neoliberal economic stance, contrasting with Mainichi Shimbun’s Keynesian view. It supports Japan’s postwar Constitution, especially Article 9, opposing changes in interpretation, including the 2014 right of collective self-defense. While retracting discredited testimonies of Seiji Yoshida in August 2014, it affirmed that women were coerced into prostitution for the Japanese military, though no official documents proved direct military recruitment on the Korean Peninsula or Taiwan, citing poverty and patriarchal systems as enabling factors. In March 2011, following criticism for aligning too closely with the government during the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster, the Asahi strengthened its investigative unit, the Tokubetsu Hodobu (Special Reports Section), which won awards in 2012 and 2013. In May 2014, it published a testimony from Masao Yoshida, the plant manager during the meltdown, stating that 90% of employees had left despite his orders, and that his instructions had not reached them. The headline “Workers Evacuated, Violating Plant Manager Orders” sparked controversy, with criticism that it implied cowardice, when many viewed the workers as heroes. Japanese journalist Ryusho Kadota criticized the mischaracterization, and the Asahi initially defended the story, demanding an apology. However, by August, the Yomiuri Shimbun, Sankei Shimbun, Kyodo News, and NHK obtained the same testimony and used it to attack the Asahi. In September, facing criticism from media and Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, the Asahi retracted the story, and president Tadakazu Kimura resigned. Reporters and editors were punished, the Special Reports Section was reduced in size, and two top reporters left to found the Tokyo Investigative Newsroom Tansa, a non-profit investigative journalism organization. The section was told to avoid Fukushima coverage and has since faded. In the evening edition of 20 April 1989, an article described damage to the world’s largest Azami coral in Okinawa, with the initial “KY” scratched, later proven to be fabricated by the Asahi photographer; president Toichiro Hitotsuyanagi resigned. On 27 September 1950, a solo interview with Japanese Communist Party executive Ritsu Ito was published, later revealed to be forged by the Asahi reporter. The Asahi Shimbun Asia Network (AAN), established in 1999, promotes information exchange in Asia and hosts annual symposia and publishes research reports; Gong Ro Myung became its president in 2003. The Asahi Prize, established in 1929 and since 1992 awarded by the Asahi Shimbun Foundation, recognizes achievements in scholarship or the arts that contribute to Japanese culture or society. Past issues are available in three forms: CD-ROMs (with headlines from 1945–1999), microfilm (from 1888), and shukusatsuban (reduced-sized print editions from 1931), widely used in research universities. The CD-ROM database includes advertisements and is accessible at Harvard-Yenching Library; researchers typically use the CD-ROM index before accessing microfilm or shukusatsuban. Issues from August 1984 onward are available through Lexis-Nexis Academic. The Asahi Shimbun was an official supporter of several Asian initiatives.

Shukusatsuban is a technology developed and popularized by the Asahi Shimbun in the 1930s to compress and archive newspapers by reducing print size so that multiple pages of a daily newspaper can fit onto a single page. These are primarily used by libraries and archives and are typically organized and released by month. Shukusatsuban resources are accessible at many leading research universities worldwide, especially those with strong Japanese studies programs. The Asahi Shimbun maintains a CD-ROM database indexing headlines and sub-headlines from 1945 to 1999. A more expensive, full-text searchable database, which includes advertisements, is available exclusively at the Harvard-Yenching Library at Harvard University. Researchers at other university libraries generally begin with the CD-ROM index and then consult microfilm or shukusatsuban versions. Microfilm versions of the Asahi Shimbun are available starting from 1888, while shukusatsuban versions begin from 1931. Issues of the Asahi Shimbun published since August 1984 are accessible through Lexis-Nexis Academic. The Asahi Shimbun has been an official supporter of several Asian Football Confederation (AFC) competitions, most recently the 2019 AFC Asian Cup. It previously sponsored both the AFC Champions League and AFC Cup until the 2018 season. The newspaper was also an official sponsor of the 2002 FIFA World Cup.
